title: Computer changed the game
content:
Hands down, this is the best AI app I have ever used. It has completely changed the way I work and has helped me build products that I never would have been able to create on my own. The results have been incredibly valuable, and the platform consistently delivers.

My only real criticism is that I wish Perplexity did a better job of helping users understand how credits and tokens work. While building my last few projects, I ended up using significantly more credits than I expected, which made the overall cost much higher than I had anticipated. The value is absolutely there, but more transparency around token usage and estimated costs would make the experience much better for users.

I would also love to see Perplexity offer a discounted plan or token program for veterans. It would be a meaningful way to support those who are using the platform to build businesses, learn new skills, and create new opportunities after military service.

Overall, despite my concerns about token transparency and pricing, I still believe Perplexity is the best AI platform available today, and I highly recommend it.

When I signed up, I figured it was a good app to use for light work with contracts and research. Everything was great at first until it was noted that I was using it a lot. Once I began getting comfortable with its functionality, it began to ask for more money for credits outside of the monthly subscription I’m already paying. “Credit’s” is what it was calling it. I fell for it a couple times but began noticing it was when I needed Information on my phone. This was one of a few issues. During the few months I was using it, I had to corrects the math it was doing for me due to the calculations being incorrect and the math wasn’t adding up correctly. I corrected it and received the common answer we’ve all come to get… “ your right to be frustrated “ or “ I see where I went wrong and will correct it”. At this point I would think that simple calculations could be done as it’s nothing more than asking it to do what a calculator does, but it messed up the math I was having it do, consistently. The other issue I have with it is its memory. I would have it write a contract with specific header info and tell it to remember it as we will be using it as a template to go by. It confirmed this request but could NEVER get it correct!
All in all, if you expect to pay for an AI assistant and get what it tells you in the advertisement, you will be disappointed. It will give you simple answers or information you ask for, but outside of it being a simple search engine… don’t expect much.
If you try and discuss these concerns with customer service, expect it to be just as frustrating as not getting the product you’ve paid for because that’s what you get. Disappointment and frustration! All in all, 1 star seems too high but it won’t let me give the half star it deserves!

title: Love the tool, but can’t afford to keep using it
content:
★★ (2/5)
I rated this tool a 5/5 before they changed their pricing and plans.

I’ve been a Pro subscriber for over a year and have spent more than $1,000 on this app because I genuinely love it. Recently I hit a spending cap on purchasing extra credits as a Pro user, and support confirmed the cap can’t be raised on Pro — the only way to increase it is upgrading to the Max plan.
Here’s the issue: I’m on Pro’s annual billing at $200/year (about $17/month). Max is $200/month. That’s not a modest step up — it’s nearly a 12x price increase, just to raise a purchase limit. I don’t need or want any of Max’s other features (the extra monthly credits, model access, etc.) — I just wanted to keep buying credits the way I always had.
If you’re a loyal Pro user who occasionally needs more credits, know that there’s no in-between option — it’s a straight leap from $17/month to $200/month, with no smaller upgrade path. I really do love this app, but I can’t justify that jump just to keep doing what I was already doing. Support was responsive and took the feedback seriously, which is the only reason this isn’t 1 star.
— Jay H.

title: Continues to impress
content:
I started with Perplexity and I keep returning to it. It continues to provide harness superiority in orchestration of models. I get more out of Claude using Perplexity. The cloud model permits me to start a conversation on one machine and follow it up later from my phone or iPad later. It does a magnificent job with Spaces (aka Projects) keeping context separated and build on by adding files for reference, etc. Each space just gets smarter.

I have developed skill.md files for processes. Perplexity actually helps me update each skill with dialogue. So if I see that my output needs improvement, I can simply ask and Perplexity will update each skill.

I pay for Pro, not Max. I found a middle ground to be able to use Perplexity Computer without paying for Max. You add your credit card and pay for credits to use Computer for specific queries as you see fit to have access to the higher level of reasoning and model selection. So I wind up paying less than the $100/month of Max, but more than the $20 of Pro.

As much as I want to be AI LLM agnostic, I keep returning to Perplexity.

title: Simply the best. Perplexity Pro
content:
There are very few things that genuinely change the way you work. For me, Perplexity Pro has been one of them.

As a Union Chief Shop Steward representing employees in the railroad transportation industry, I carry a tremendous responsibility. My work isn’t based on opinions—it depends on facts, evidence, contract language, labor law, NLRB decisions, arbitration principles, and careful research. Every grievance, every Request for Information, every bargaining proposal, and every recommendation I make can directly affect someone’s job, benefits, or livelihood.

Perplexity has become much more than a search engine. It’s like having a research partner available whenever I need one. It helps me work through complex collective bargaining agreements, analyze company policies, review thousands of pages of documents, understand labor law, identify relevant legal authority, and ask better questions before I ever present an argument.

Outside of union work, it has become part of my everyday life. I use it to research investments and financial planning, understand medical studies and treatment options, explore history, learn new technology, and satisfy my curiosity about almost anything. It has helped me become a more informed advocate, a better decision-maker, and a lifelong learner.

The biggest difference isn’t that it gives me answers—it’s that it helps me think more deeply. It encourages me to verify information, consider different perspectives, and build stronger, evidence-based conclusions.

Technology is only as valuable as the way you use it. For me, Perplexity has become one of the most valuable tools I’ve ever added to my professional and personal life. It has saved me countless hours, strengthened my work, and allowed me to focus more of my energy on what truly matters: representing people fairly, making informed decisions, and never stopping the pursuit of knowledge.

Thank you, Perplexity, for building a tool that has genuinely made a difference in my life.

title: Wasted credits on an unusable result
content:
I paid for additional credits to complete a specific document redesign project, but the result was extremely disappointing. The instructions were clear: use the existing redesigned intake packet as the base and make cosmetic/layout fixes only. Instead, the system rewrote and condensed regulated healthcare/legal content, changed clinical language, added or altered sections, and produced a version that was not safe to use without major review.

This was not a creative writing task. It was a healthcare intake packet where wording matters. I needed layout cleanup: fix text overlap, improve readability, keep the packet black-and-white, center headings, keep signatures inside boxes, and preserve the original legal content. Instead, the output changed the substance of consent forms, HIPAA-related acknowledgments, client rights, financial policy language, and clinical screening content.

The design improved visually, but the actual deliverable became unusable because it no longer matched the source documents. For a paid continuation, that is unacceptable. It cost time, money, and created more cleanup work instead of solving the problem.

I will not use this service again for document production or any project requiring careful adherence to instructions.

author: pedestrianperspectives

title: Bait‑and‑switch limits and unhelpful support
content:
If I could rate this zero stars I would. I signed up for the paid Pro plan specifically to use file/image uploads for my summer classes (A&P and microbiology). I’m in a 4‑week block class, so every day counts, and I was relying on this app to analyze screenshots and course materials to help make study guides for me.
At first it worked, then suddenly I started seeing an “uploads remaining this month” message and hit a hard wall where the upload button was greyed out. Instead of a clear explanation of what the limits are, the app just pushed me to upgrade to a higher tier (Max) – even though I was already paying for Pro. There is no upfront, honest disclosure of concrete upload limits, and they clearly changed the behavior after I had already subscribed.
Support was worse than the product. I got canned responses explaining that free plans have limits and I should upgrade, even after I repeatedly told them I was already on Pro. When they finally acknowledged my plan, they still refused to give any specific numbers for the limits and basically said, “upgrade for more.” No real transparency, no ownership, no useful fix. Just upsell.
On top of that, the AI itself frequently ignored what I actually asked, forced me to correct it over and over, and still gave wrong or inconsistent information about its own features and limits. When you’re paying for a tool to help with an intensive class, that’s not just annoying – it wastes time you don’t have.
If you’re considering paying for this expecting reliable uploads and clear terms, be careful. The way they change limits without clearly telling you, hide the actual numbers, and then push you toward more expensive tiers feels like a bait‑and‑switch. I’ll be taking my business elsewhere

title: Powerful Research, Rough Edges
content:
The engine here is legitimately great at research. It shows its work as it searches, cites real sources inline, and the Deep Research reports are impressive. For anyone who needs fast, credible answers with copious amounts of source information, Perplexity is definitely worth a look.

But the daily experience has real frustrations. The UI shifts constantly — features move, disappear, or get renamed without warning. There's a pattern of capabilities being promoted then quietly limited or paywalled, which gets old fast. The Artifacts feature crashes often enough that I can't rely on it when I actually need it.

If Perplexity stabilized what it already has, it'd be a 5-star app without question. Right now it feels like a brilliant research tool still figuring out what it wants to be.

author: JaySalay

title: Far behind ChatGPT, Gemini & Claude
content:
I subscribed to Perplexity AI, tried the app once, and immediately regretted it. The AI struggled to understand basic questions and constantly needed multiple follow-up prompts just to figure out what I was asking. With apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, I have rarely had that issue even with the free versions. The experience felt clunky, unintuitive, and honestly far behind the competition. No other experience with AI has ranked lower than this.

The worst part wasn’t even the AI quality it was customer support. I requested a refund almost immediately after realizing the service wasn’t for me. Over the last Two Months I’ve exchanged more than 15 emails with support. Every response says someone will “reach out shortly,” but nobody ever does. Then I follow up again and get the exact same copy & paste response.

There’s no phone number, no real escalation process, and apparently no intention of actually resolving customer issues. I paid for a service I was not able to benefit from and ended up spending much of my free time following up with Sam from perplexity support who ultimately refused to help.

Don’t risk your time, money or mental space on trying this app. Support other easier to use apps that value their customers.

title: Updated: Almost Perfect
content:
I’m a long time perplexity Pro subscriber and have seen Perplexity go from my most useful and delightful app to my most inconsistent and infuriating app and back to near perfect. The dip was caused by botched changes to Deep Research which were either reversed or somehow adjusted back to usefulness. I’m happy to report that with this fix, perplexity is again a delight to use — but not perfect.

The one issue I am facing now is the baffling decision to restrict Perplexity CarPlay from chats in your chat history. This seems like a feature designed by people who believe that users are only interested in information pertaining to new things and don’t spend time reflecting on / researching / refining / building upon past ideas or projects. For me, this limitation makes Perplexity CarPlay useless — so I reluctantly use ChatGPT CarPlay which wisely does not have this restriction. Fix this shortcoming and Perplexity gets 5 stars from this fan.

title: Only ONE true complaint
content:
1. Mode clarity on desktop is poor
•The UI makes it hard to see at a glance whether you’re in Ask vs Computer, especially on larger screens where the dropdown and labels are subtle.
•The mode selector looks like a generic “+/options” button instead of a high‑stakes toggle that controls whether credits are consumed.
2. Defaulting to Computer feels deceptive when credits are limited
•On my laptop, the default experience shifted into Computer / Max without my explicit intent.
•Because I didn’t explicitly know “this mode consumes a scarce credit pool,” my entire allowance was exhausted in under 72 hours (first time use on laptop).
3. Credits should be impossible to use accidentally
•Any first Computer use on a new device should:
•Clearly state “This uses credits; you have X remaining this month,” and
•Require a one‑time explicit opt‑in (checkbox or confirm) before enabling Computer as a default.
•The current design allows high‑cost usage to be triggered by normal interaction patterns (clicking the default mode) without understanding the cost.
4. Clearer separation of “subscription” vs “credits”
•As a Pro subscriber, you reasonably expected your core usage to be covered by your monthly fee.
•The distinction between “Pro subscription is fine” vs “Computer credits are gone” is not obvious in the UI. It just feels like “my Pro stopped working and is asking me to upgrade again,” which erodes trust. (Chrome browser on laptop; app on phone)

title: A Total Scam: Fake Model Claims, Hidden Limits, and No Accountability, What they sell you do not get
content:
I don’t usually leave reviews like this, but my experience with Perplexity has been frustrating enough that people should know what they’re getting into.

I signed up based on their advertised “bundled” access to multiple AI models, including ones like Grok and Kimi K2. I was explicitly told these were included—but in practice, they were either unavailable or not actually what was being used. That leads to a bigger issue: transparency. The platform often shows one model name, but when tested, it doesn’t behave like that model at all. In some cases, it even appeared to switch models mid-session, which completely wrecks consistency—especially if you’re doing serious work like research or long-form writing.

When I reached out for support, my concerns were mostly dismissed or ignored. No real answers, no accountability.

Another major problem is their wrapper system. Because it forces heavy sourcing, the AI ends up parroting citations instead of actually thinking through problems. The responses feel constrained, shallow, and overly filtered—more like stitched-together summaries than real reasoning.

On top of that, the “bundle deal” itself feels misleading. There are strict limits on input length and uploads—limitations that don’t exist when using these models directly elsewhere. So you’re not really getting what you think you’re paying for.

The few models that do seem available are heavily restricted with aggressive guardrails, making them difficult to use for deeper research or nuanced analysis. If your goal is serious writing or exploration, this becomes a major roadblock.

Bottom line: I ended up paying separately for direct access to models elsewhere, and the difference is night and day. Based on my experience, this service overpromises and underdelivers.

I’d strongly recommend doing your homework before subscribing.

title: Fantastic Research Tool with a Few Usability Quirks
content:
No arguments here — the functionality is spectacular. Perplexity’s research abilities are truly amazing and have become my go-to for in-depth queries.
That said, there are a few quirks in the iOS app that I hope the team addresses soon:
•  Chat scrolling issue: Every time you reopen a chat (even very long ones), it always loads at the very top. You’re forced to scroll all the way down to pick up where you left off. The quick-jump arrow button helps a bit but often stops halfway instead of going to the bottom.
•  Copying text problem: When trying to select and copy text from a response, the chat sometimes suddenly closes and returns you to the main chat list, losing your place.
•  Occasional freezing: The app has hung or frozen more than once, requiring a full restart.
I absolutely love using Perplexity and rely on it daily. These small deficiencies are the only things holding back an otherwise outstanding experience. Hoping the team can smooth them out soon — keep up the great work!

author: Atxmob

title: LLM in use
content:
Subject: Request: Always show active LLM/model in iOS/iPad app UI
Message:
I’m a Perplexity Pro subscriber using the native iOS app on iPad. One of the main reasons I pay for Perplexity is access to multiple top LLMs and intelligent routing (Best mode, etc.), as you describe in your Pro documentation and marketing.[perplexity +1]
However, in the iPad app there is no clear indication of which LLM is currently being used on the main query screen. I do not see any visible model name (e.g., Best, GPT, Claude, Gemini, Sonar) near the input, nor an obvious place to change or confirm the active model per thread. This makes it hard to trust and reason about answers, and it undercuts the value of having multiple models at all.
On web, recent updates appear to move in the right direction by surfacing model names and giving more transparency around Model Council and other advanced modes, but this hasn’t reached the iPad UI in a usable way.[perplexity +1]
Feature request:
1.	Always show the currently active model/mode (e.g., “Best (multi‑model)”, “Claude 4.6 Sonnet”, “GPT‑5.2”, “Gemini”, “Sonar”) prominently in the main input area on iOS/iPadOS.
2.	Make it obvious and one‑tap to change the model/mode for new threads, and clearly indicate if Best is automatically routing between models.
3.	Add a platform‑specific help article or inline tooltip: “On iOS/iPadOS, here’s how to see and change your model.”
For a Pro user, not knowing which LLM is answering a query feels like a serious UX gap. Please prioritize improving model visibility and selection on iPad.

title: From 5‑star potential to a 3‑star reality: please fix limits and stability
content:
I really want to like this app, and I’m not giving up on it yet, but my first day with Pro has been a rollercoaster. The core strengths are real: search + news/article summaries are excellent, citations are helpful, and access to multiple frontier models in one place is genuinely valuable.
The problem is everything around the “flagship” features like Deep Research and Labs (creating files/apps). They are promoted as key reasons to upgrade, but in practice the quotas feel extremely small and disappear after just a few serious uses, with no clear, honest numbers shown up front. Calling this “dynamic limits” doesn’t change how frustrating it feels as a paying user who upgraded specifically to try these features.
On top of that, the overall experience still has rough edges and occasional bugs, which makes it even more painful when every Deep/Labs run seems to “burn” a precious hidden quota. It’s hard not to feel misled when the marketing sets high expectations, but the reality is “you get to properly try it a handful of times and then you’re done for the period.”
I’m giving 3 stars because the underlying technology and information experience are strong, and I can see the potential if they are more transparent and generous with limits and improve stability. But right now, it feels like a 5‑star engine trapped in a 3‑star product experience. Please:
•	clearly disclose realistic usage limits for Deep Research and Labs,
•	make the quotas less restrictive for paying users,
•	and fix the reliability issues.
If those things improve, this would easily become one of the best AI tools on my phone.

title: Politically Biased!
content:
Let’s get something straight. I’m not a Republican, Democrat, or Independent. I’m a Constitutionalist. I only care about what’s best for the people, the country, and the U.S. Constitution. With that out of the way, here’s my story: I asked this app why there’s so much tension between Colombia and the United States. It instantly blamed Donald Trump. Now, I’m in my fifties and I can tell you the relationship has been rocky for decades, way before Trump was even a blip on the political radar. When I pointed that out, it finally gave the right answer, but not before acting like a political comedian who thinks every problem started with the last president. I’ve noticed this app, like most trendy AI assistants, leans heavily left when all I want is a truthful answer. It’s like asking for directions and getting a lecture on climate change. These apps need to stop leaning so heavily on either side of the political spectrum. They should just give us the facts, not a political sermon. It’s ridiculous that I have to fact check my fact checker.

Oh, and the memory on this thing is a joke. It forgets everything I say five seconds later. I could tell it my favorite color, my dog’s name, and my life story, and it would still ask me the same questions over and over. It’s like talking to a goldfish with a PhD. If you’re going to charge for this, at least make it remember something. This is not just annoying. It’s a deal breaker. If the memory doesn’t improve, I’d rather chat with a brick wall. If I wanted a forgetful, politically biased robot, I’d just hang out with my toaster.

title: Great but needs improvement
content:
As a ChatGPT subscriber, I can say that Perplexity Pro has some impressive advantages. Its strengths include deep searching, the option to choose between longer legacy models, and more powerful online, up-to-date search resources for your questions.

The main drawback, however, is user-friendliness. It’s surprisingly difficult to find my previous threads and return to them later when I want to resume a topic or project. Ironically, a tool built for deep search lacks a simple internal search function for its own content.

That said, I still find Perplexity useful for in-depth searching and more complex reasoning questions. For reference, I’ve been a ChatGPT subscriber for over a year, and I’ve been using Perplexity Pro for about a week. I really hope the developers focus on improving organization and adding internal thread search to make the experience more seamless.

title: I can’t believe how broken the Perplexity iPad app still is after all this time.
content:
The biggest issue? Every time you accidentally tap outside the chat window while typing, the window vanishes and everything you wrote disappears. Your entire question, gone. And on an iPad, this happens constantly — you’re always adjusting your grip or the angle, and it’s so easy to tap the wrong spot. There’s more screen room to miss the chat window than there is actual chat window, so be ready to be more frustrated than not.

It’s not just accidental taps either. Switch to check a message? Gone. Get a notification? Gone. Put the iPad down for a minute? Also gone. Blinked more than usual? Of course, gone! Say something the model disapproves of? Definitely gone!!

The app has zero ability to retain what you’re working on when this happens, or to only close the window when the user actually wants to close it. It should be able to keep your draft even after closing the window.

This makes it completely unusable for anything longer than a few words. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve typed out a detailed question only to watch it vanish because I touched the screen wrong. And most of the time, what’s lost is irreplaceable.

I’ve basically given up on the app entirely. Just seeing the icon on my screen annoys me now because I know it’s going to frustrate me if I try to use it. So I just pick a different option.

The crazy part is these seem like such obvious problems. How has no one at Perplexity actually tried using their own app on an iPad? It would take about 2 minutes to discover these issues.

I really want to like this app, but right now it’s just broken. Fix the text input handling, and I’ll happily change this review, but until then, it’s a hard pass.

Note: When you select a different model to rewrite an answer, it loses all context from the conversation and acts like you’re starting fresh. This makes the rewrite function completely useless.

title: Hard to follow
content:
Perplexity AI currently presents chat history in a continuous text format without visually distinguishing user messages from AI responses with different sides, fonts, or bubbles like ChatGPT does. This makes it harder to quickly see who said what when you revisit the conversation later.
To make it easier, a possible solution would be for Perplexity to implement a chat interface design similar to ChatGPT, where user inputs appear on one side (e.g., right) and AI responses appear on the other (e.g., left) with distinct text styles. This visual differentiation helps users quickly scan and identify their messages versus the AI’s replies.
Unfortunately, there isn’t a user-facing setting to change this layout in Perplexity at the moment.

Same goes for Google, Facebook, etc. These days you just can't get away from the hacker syndrome, but we have to count on app providers to at least make an effort. Other than that, solid 5/5.

Also, when you paste a big query, or some data, it gets attached to the query, but there’s no way to access that pasted text and data on iPhone, so you can’t repeat your query. I’d say user attachments could be included in assets and it would be nice

Basically, I made a big prompt and got a great app with minor issues and wasn’t able to fix the minor issues because I ran the wrong query type because I forgot it automatically changes and then when I went back the thing was stuck in a different contextual mode

title: started sending random push notifications
content:
The app tells you to enable push notifications to receive a notification when a long-running query completes. This feature doesn’t work. Instead, Perplexity just starts sending random news stories as push notifications.
There is no opt-in to news story notifications; they just start sending them when you enable the (broken) long-running query notifications. There is no opt-out option either; you have to disable all push notification permissions to stop them.

title: Powerful, intuitive and localized!
content:
I have been using Pepexility on my iPhone, App on Mac and through Browsers for few months and here's a clear summary of the key points about Perplexity Pro with its new features:

Enhanced Capabilities: Perplexity Pro now integrates two powerful AI tools: Deepseek R1, based in the US, and OpenAI's o3-mini. This combination offers users improved performance, faster responses, and a wider range of capabilities.

Deepseek R1: Known for handling complex tasks, especially in reasoning and coding. Offers faster response times and improved accuracy, ideal for detailed research and technical queries. Hosting in the US provides better data privacy and compliance with local regulations.

OpenAI o3-mini: Designed for quick, efficient tasks with lightning-fast responses, making it great for everyday queries and fact-checking. Cost-effective and suitable for devices with limited resources, but not ideal for very complex queries.

User Experience: The platform maintains a user-friendly interface, allowing easy switching between models based on your needs.  Provides versatility for different use cases, from in-depth research to quick checks. I like how it suggests follow up questions after a query which is very helpful to dive deeper into certains topics of interest.

Who Should Consider It:

Professionals, researchers, and developers who need precise, fast, and reliable information. Users who value speed for simple tasks might prefer the o3-mini, while those needing deeper analysis might find Deepseek R1 more beneficial.

Considerations:

Deepseek R1 can be verbose at times. The Pro version might be costly for smaller teams or individual users unless they fully use its advanced features.

Overall, Perplexity Pro with Deepseek R1 and OpenAI o3-mini provides a high-value experience for those needing top-notch AI capabilities, despite being on the pricier side.

author: NKipper

title: The Apex in GAI Research Companions
content:
Perplexity is its best as a systematic researcher. It shines at object differentiation (such as when you upload photos), parsing and ranking research legitimacy, and sticking to objective language output. Your ability to select the model (i.e. Claude, Llama, GPT4, etc.) provides an additional layer of customization of output. With new features such as “deep research”, you can choose the extent to which you want the available online body scoured.

It’s clear the developers are working on more multi-layering and I would not be surprised if a custom research-focus search engine is launched that combines the interface of a search engine with the current GAI call-and-response presentation.

I see unique product differentiation with perplexity, compared to the more “conversational” GAI apps. If I am a user interested in GAI applications, I would source both, with Perplexity’s utility coming in the aforementioned research-based investigations - such as academic-meets-practical quandries such as in science, engineering, medicine, general instruction, and everyday solution formulation and true/false/facts of the matter questions.

author: Zahinsarwar

title: Useful AI
content:
I find Perplexity to be the most useful AI application I have tried, and I’ve tried a bunch. The answers it gives to questions, both simple and complex, are thorough, sober, mostly error-free, and useful. I can go back and retrieve an old answer easily. I can examine its sources if an answer surprises me.

Perplexity uses different underlying technologies and is always updating its methods. I feel that I get the benefit of advances without constantly switching platforms.

I do find that the answers I receive are dependent on how I ask the questions. So I try to put my questions precisely and sometimes I will ask the question in a different way to see how the answer changes. The occasional error is usually the byproduct of a sloppy question.

An example might help. I was interested in seeing how development shifted in the ancient world. I used population size of major centers as a proxy. So I was asking Perplexity where was the first city to pass 10,000 inhabitants, 25,000, 50,000, etc. When I asked which city first reached 250,000 it gave me possibly Alexandria in 1 AD or Teotihuacan in 450 AD. That’s clearly wrong because Rome already had over a million inhabitants sometime in the 2nd century BCE. But I had been sloppy. Putting the question as “which city first had at least 250,000 inhabitants” yields a much more useful answer.

Anyway, my fiancee and I are always researching something or other and we both have found Perplexity, or Earnest as she likes to call it because of its tone, immensely useful.

I find Perplexity to be the most useful AI application I have tried, and I’ve tried a bunch. The answers it gives to questions, both simple and complex, are thorough, sober, mostly error-free, and useful. I can go back and retrieve an old answer easily. I can examine its sources if an answer surprises me.

Perplexity uses different underlying technologies and is always updating its methods. I feel that I get the benefit of advances without constantly switching platforms.

I do find that the answers I receive are dependent on how I ask the questions. So I try to put my questions precisely and sometimes I will ask the question in a different way to see how the answer changes. The occasional error is usually the byproduct of a sloppy question.

An example might help. I was interested in seeing how development shifted in the ancient world. I used population size of major centers as a proxy. So I was asking Perplexity where was the first city to pass 10,000 inhabitants, 25,000, 50,000, etc. When I asked which city first reached 250,000 it gave me possibly Alexandria in 1 AD or Teotihuacan in 450 AD. That’s clearly wrong because Rome already had over a million inhabitants sometime in the 2nd century BCE. But I had been sloppy. Putting the question as “which city first had at least 250,000 inhabitants” yields a much more useful answer.

Anyway, my fiancee and I are always researching something or other and we both have found Perplexity, or Earnest as she likes to call it because of its tone, immensely useful.

Oh, and I like its built-in news service: articles I find interesting and which don’t move me despair.

author: Kevbot111

title: Really good with some shortcomings
content:
I really love this app. I use it every day and recommend it to friends, and love that it cites its sources.

However, I’ve been running into some issues which have gotten worse in recent week: my searches often get timed out and my queries erased. I often have to try multiple times before it works. It’s gotten to the point where I don’t trust that anything I submit will work, so I instinctually copy my query before submitting it so I don’t have to type it over.

Another issue is that sometimes the results are just wrong. When I point this out and ask it to try again it apologizes but gives the same wrong answer over and over again. This happened recently when I was asking it to fetch and comment on the content of a tweet, so maybe this is an issue on x’s side.

If it weren’t for these issues I’d give Perplexity five stars. Hopefully these can get addressed!

content: I’m a data science/ai manager. I spend most of my workday leading integrations and development with AI. So I’m very critical of AI apps. The app offers many of features I look for (easy thread management, the ability to select different models, decent markdown rendering, etc.), and it’s built around a web search functionality that I think is best in class. I still wouldn’t blame someone for using ChatGPT as their go-to app, but if it’s not one of these two then I can honestly say they are missing out.

title: SO BAD！！！
content: I feel compelled to express my profound disappointment with the Perplexity application's abysmal user experience. Are the developers merely going through the motions without any genuine commitment to quality? This level of performance is absolutely beneath the standards one would expect from a modern application. The current state of the mobile application is nothing less than a testament to poor execution and questionable professional standards.

author: H20242024

title: Perplexity Pro was a waste of my $$
content:
I have used Perplexity free version ever since it was released, and it’s great for certain queries, but abysmal for others, as it constantly relays outdated information.

I became so tired of the app’s apologies (the only thing it always got right) that recently I sprang for the $200 Perplexity Pro. But there’s not really any relief. For an app that claims to have up-to-date ability, I’m so shocked at how often—in fact, the majority of my queries—I have to tell it to go back and look again, even for simple answers, like how to return to the previous channel on an Apple TV Remote. This $200 app CONSISTENTLY gives outdated info, as if it’s a lazy basement dweller who hates taking out the trash. It’s just plain lazy.

But it sure is good at apologizing.

author: jginfl

title: A Research Assistant for All
content: I first engaged with AI when it was first released to the public a bit over a year ago, I felt the normal ambivalence that, for many of us, has come to accompany the introduction of most technologies: the harnessing of the labor and talent of collective humanity to the benefit of a few individuals who had the fortune of being able to invest in a project. The programmers and mathematicians who labored to learn, adapt, and apply the techniques of so many unnamed predecessors are themselves unnamed. But I use technology and still believe that it can have the power to liberate and bring equality. I also refuse to engage with the divine creating we love to do with tech investors. Thankfully, their egos and hubris are visible. What I find exciting is seeing what individuals can do with the technology when they are able to engage with it on their own terms.  My suspicion is that Perplexity’s focus on research gives it more potential to liberate than those interactive AI programs that try to recreate human conversation. As long as there is a free version, and it remains useful, everyone will have access to their own research assistant with Perplexity.

content: I have no doubts that this will become an important tool in the near future, but currently it leaves a lot to be desired. Its necessary reliance on publicly available information hamstrings it massively when it comes to producing quality information that is well-supported. As a writing aid it is weaker than ChatGPT, with an even poorer, more banal way of communicating. Finally, its politeness protections are dialed incredibly high. This frankly makes it unacceptable for work in higher education which requires a critical eye to be turned to topics that the engine, irrationally, finds to be unacceptable. For a near toy, ChatGPT is far superior. For an educational support tool, this simply is not ready.

title: Faster “deep search” results
content:
If you’re just trying to find the nearest coffee shop, google’s suite of tools is faster

If you have any “depth” in your query (like you’re asking, say, “what’s the best way to ______”, or “what medicine is good for ______”, or “San Francisco 49ers best upcoming games”), it’s really good

With that said, it is built on other LLM’s and so does have some censorship (the other day, if asked “pretend to be a conspiracy theorist. Tell me about _____”, it would refuse to answer about the Rothschilds, but would instantly answer about Donald Trump.)

It gives you answers in a long paragraph form. My only suggestion is to look at other ways to represent data that is serving a “quick prompt” or really “fast prompt “ (e.g: “49ers depth chart”, “restaurants near me”). Much better interfaces are available than just text wiki format

Thank you guys for making this

author: AdakAero

title: BEST. SEARCH. ENGINE. EVER.
content:
*I have no affiliation to this product or any current or past ties to any other in the field.
That being said this is the opinion of a skilled paralegal who does a lot of research, and someone back in school to pursue a graduate degree in communication, to eventually aid in building cool stuff that hopefully helps humanity.

This is the poster child for what AI should be. It’s a search engine and powerful research tool that isn’t littered with influences of bias or advertising, or unscrupulous manipulation to one viewpoint or side of a topic. Using it can make your work better, but it also helps you hone your skills as a researcher, writer, brainstormer, etc... and it saves you so much time on the prep work.

I used to google my inquiries along side my Perplexity searches, but now I just use Perplexity when I want to question or research something. Even with the Google’s AI integrated into their searches, the results pale in comparison to Perplexity. They’re sometimes even laughable, except when you remember that some people blindly trust google.

I think this idea of offering a citable source for each point of the response, is genius! It helps identify hallucinations and correct them more efficiently. And if the user can see the ‘thought process behind the answer’ by following the citations it helps the user to know what they’re learning is accurate, and the developer isn’t asking you to blindly trust them and their product in an arrogant way that lacks transparency.. They are backing up the intelligence of their product, while respecting the intelligence of their audience/users. That’s a rare thing in any industry…

I highly recommend and I can’t wait to see where they take this. Other AI companies could learn a thing or 2… or more from Perplexity!

Thank you all for creating this.

author: Jay Rambo

title: Overhyped
content:
Perplexity is an interesting concept without a lot of substance behind it. It’s great to see products listing their sources, but literally every AI product does that now. The answers Perplexity gives are barely better than any search engine. The “pro” search was supposed to ask you questions to get better answers once upon a time, but rarely seems to do anything like that now.

At $20/mo the subscription is overpriced. If you are interested in privacy and advanced search features, you’d be better off investing your money into a privacy first browser with AI features built in. There are some good ones out there now that offer great experiences that aren’t just a AI chat bot that can use the web.

It seems like Perplexity was one of thousands of products that rose quickly during the current AI boom designed to quickly soak up attention and then flounder when people realize it’s only slightly different than a search engine.

title: Great for Consensus Answers + Follow-up
content:
Pros:
* See review title. Logical follow-ups are also suggested, which I find quite handy.
* Answers are clear and concise, in plain English.
* It’s as fast as google.
* History of questions is maintained for returning to topic, and easily deleted as desired.
* Zero click bait to distract you. Reminds me of google 15 years ago.
* Sources used for consensus information are clearly displayed, and seem to be high-end reliable (NIH, CDC, Mayo Clinic etc.)
* Queries are not sent until you hit the “go” arrow, making it easy to read and rephrase as appropriate. For some, this could be a con since it’s an added step, but I prefer it. It leads to more precise, efficient answers.

Con’s:
I haven’t found any to date. But, since nothing is perfect, 4 stars (I’m a very hard grader).

Perhaps it’s simplicity will bother some but, as previously stated, I really like that. Search interfaces are overly complex these days, and filled with invasive, self-serving advertising disguised as entertainment or knowledge.

title: The way google used to be
content:
I’m giving this 4 instead of 5 because the last few updates have been following a worrying trend that makes me fear perplexity will go the way of most apps and downgrade to the point of being a shadow of its former self. It’s been many many years since I stopped bothering to look anything up on google because of the terrible unrelated results. But then came perplexity - free, no passwords and logins, just direct and accurate answers to your questions in a half second. Every time. No fuss, no sponsored results. I think of it as AI that basically scours a google search result and instantly weeds out the garbage and irrelevant info and quickly and accurately gives you the answer to your question. No fuss no muss. Makes searching the web useful and fast again. I use it every day. Multiple times. For all types of questions. And I recommend it to everyone. That said - I hope they don’t keep changing it or go the path of most excellent apps and break what isn’t broken. Still the best thing to happen to the web since old school google. De-clutters and intelligently searches search engines and gets straight to the point. Amazing and should be the number one app priority for everyone.

author: Denise1986az

title: Quality of responses continues to go down
content:
I don’t know if it’s the model, or the search engine, but where I used to get detailed responses, compiled from multiple sources that were all actually relevant, I now get a short and superficial summary of what appear to be just the top search results.

Worse, I sometimes get answers that show that the model isn’t adequately parsing the input. For example: a question about Canon laser printer cartridges returns what appears to be a mash-up of quotes from various printer companies’ marketing materials, for both laser and ink-jet printers, rather than about the relevant toner cartridges I asked about.

And worst of all, I now sometimes get responses that are nothing but the question restated, then completely unrelated gibberish, followed by a “summary paragraph” that just restates the restated question with the gibberish mixed in. It’s baffling!

Oh, and some of the guardrails in place, I suspect to avoid liability, get in the way of meaningful results. I asked it if a particular company, widely reputed to have unreliable products, made reliable products. It replied enthusiastically “Yes! XCorp makes very reliable products!” I asked for examples of their products that were unreliable and it started the response with “XCorp makes very reliable products!” and then went on to list a bunch of examples of their products being unreliable.
Hallucinations, indeed.

I’ll keep the app around because it’s still fun to play with, but I certainly won’t be using it for any meaningful searches unless I see some improvement in the quality of the responses.

author: DawnRoeske.art

title: Good but badly needs specific UX improvement
content:
This is more feature request than review.

Devs, please consider the following UX improvements as urgently needed:

1) The prompt field is currently limited to one line. This makes entering long prompts very clunky. The app needs a multi line prompt input field.

2) It’s easy to accidentally clear a prompt, and there is no undo or shake-to-undo. This is a big time waster. The app needs an undo for prompt clears.

3) Reply text cannot current be selected and copied. This greatly slows down many cases of iterative prompting or otherwise rising text from the reply. All prompt and reply text needs to be selectable so that sections can be copied ad hoc.

Collectively, these issues mean that a power user greatly benefit from writing prompts in a separate text editor and pasting them over into Perplexity. Clearly this is not ideal - a text based UI needs to have excellent text manipulation UX.

Thanks for taking these humble suggestions on board!

title: Know the answer before asking the question
content:
Too often, Perplexity gives wrong answers to research questions, and falsely interprets soft conclusions from hard information.

It takes too many shortcuts to arrive at answers too quickly, providing results that are skewed or wrong between 50 and 80 percent of the time.

While very valuable in many respects, Perplexity ends up wasting substantial  customer time on research projects because the user has to challenge answers that are not supported by the sources it cites.
